Viewed Did you know 90% of people with high blood pressure are told it’s “essential hypertension” — meaning doctors don’t even know the cause? Yet you’re handed medications with side effects like fatigue, dizziness… even brain shrinkage over time.

Let’s clear things up. 👇

When you have high blood pressure, it’s not random. It’s your body trying to compensate for underlying imbalances — things like:
🔷 Low potassium, magnesium, or vitamin D
🔷 Poor liver or gut health
🔷 Processed foods, alcohol, and stress
💊 The Problem with Medications:

 Calcium channel blockers shrink your brain, ACE inhibitors cause chronic cough, and aspirin? Latest studies show little to no benefit.

🌿 Natural Ways to Support Blood Pressure:
 🔷 Eat potassium-packed leafy greens and veggies
 🔷 Load up on garlic and celery to boost nitric oxide
 🔷 Try L-arginine for blood vessel support
 🔷 Vitamin D3, magnesium, and tocotrienols for heart health
 🔷 Consider natural beta-blockers like L-theanine from green tea

Fix the root cause. Give your arteries what they need. Take care of your stress. Rebuild your health the natural way. 🩺💙

Many of my friends privately tell me that they're not having much sex, fertility markers are alarmingly bad, nighttime erections are rare and when they do want sex, they can't perform as desired. 

Their conditions are typical of current culture: chronic sleep deprivation, high stress, and a poor diet. And they're fighting with low-grade to severe depression or anxiety. 

Whether they like it or not, they're locked into a never-ending race of status, power and wealth.

It requires them to be on 24/7. No matter how hard they work, the constant social-media comparisons invites them to feel perpetually inadequate, unseen and insufficiently respected. 

These private conversations mirror population data: 

+ global fertility dropped over 50% in 50 yrs
+ sperm counts down over 50% since 70s
+ 30% of 20s men had no sexual intimacy past year
+ 83 million Americans are chronically sleep deprived 
+ 4-5 hrs phone time day, checking 58 times
+ ~43% of Americans are obese 

They know things are not well but they don't know what to do. 

This is why I talk about nighttime erections. They are as important a biomarker as blood pressure, cholesterol or blood glucose. 

If your body is not naturally generating 3-5 robust erections per night, your body is telling you something is not right. 

Tell someone to sleep more and eyes roll. Call their attention to the fact that their dick is broken and they tune in.

Women, this applies to you as well: you, too, experience nighttime genital arousal and are subject to the same risks. 

Our current culture is a sick culture. We've sold our souls to a system that martyrs us in exchange for its progress. We mistakenly believe that we are its victors when we are in fact it's disposable tools. 

Culture is changing and soon this will all be very obvious. Health will become the priority. Existence will become the highest virtue. 

I'm not arguing that you shouldn't work hard or be ambitions. Quite the opposite. 

I'm arguing that you should be even more ambitious. That no generation of humans could ever be as ambitious as we can now. I'm arguing that its intelligent and wise to make health your number one life priority because without, you're an old school martyr and that's not cool. 

Do yourself a favor, see this before it's too late for you to be part of this era of being human.

They look for unicorns.

Viewed Avoid high intensity exercise 4 hours before sleep.
It impairs sleep and recovery according to a new study. 

Study (from WHOOP) found that late night exercise... 
- Delayed sleep onset
- Shorter total sleep duration
- Lower sleep quality
- Higher resting heart rate (RHR)
- Decreased heart rate variability (HRV)

More details
• Sleep onset

Even workouts ending 6 hours before bed delayed sleep if they were high or maximal strain.

Maximal intensity at 2 hours before bed = 36-minute delay in falling asleep vs. light exercise.

• Sleep duration

Exercise within 6–2 hours of bedtime associated with shorter night sleep, the higher the intensity the shorter the sleep duration. 

Max effort at 2 hours before bedtime = 22.2 minutes less sleep, on average.

• RHR + HRV
Throughout the day, higher intensity = higher RHR and lower HRV. (Indicating less nighttime recovery)

Starting at 4 hours before bedtime, all types of exercise affected recovery markers.

Highest intensity exercise effort at 2 hours before bedtime = RHR up by 3.9 bpm (6.8%), HRV down by 32.6%. 

Takeaway:
You might think your 9PM training session is productive. But your nervous system disagrees, and your sleep suffers.

Viewed Are There Hidden Toxins in Your Food? 🧪

Food labels don’t always tell the full story. Even if something seems healthy on the surface, it may contain ingredients that aren’t clearly listed—or aren’t regulated at all.

Here’s what to watch for:

🚨 The “Rounding Rule”
If a food contains less than 0.5g (500 mg) of an ingredient per serving, companies can round it down to zero—meaning it doesn’t have to appear on the label.

❌ Over 200 Names for Sugar
Sugar hides under dozens of names like dextrose, maltodextrin, and syrup solids. Even “sugar-free” products may contain starches that spike blood sugar.

🧫 Hexane in Plant-Based Foods
Hexane is a chemical solvent used in soy protein isolate processing—found in many bars, shakes, and meat alternatives. Though it’s a known neurotoxin, it isn’t currently regulated in food manufacturing.

🔍 How to Spot Hidden Starch
Want to test it yourself? Add a drop of iodine to water mixed with the product. If it turns blue, it likely contains starch.

The bottom line: Don’t just read the front of the label—check the ingredients list, and know what to look for.

Viewed A feudal lord bit the dust because he didn’t know how to ask people a favor 😂.

In the mid-16th century, the Sué family took control of a chunk of land in western Japan after overthrowing the feudal lord who was their employer. Treachery 😫!

A colleague of theirs, the Mōri samurai family, was related to the dead employer and therefore sided against the Sué family. Revenge 😠!

So the Sués set out with over 20,000 men and 500 warships to destroy the Mōris who just had up to 3,500 men protecting a tiny fort they had built on Miyajima Island. You didn’t need to be a rocket scientist to figure out who was going to be annihilated. 

Prior to the battle, both the Sué family and Mōri family had consulted an infamous group of pirates called the Murakami Pirates. They were the most adept naval fighters in all of Japan, and allying them was crucial for victory. 

The Mōri family had sent diplomats to the Murakami pirates and pleaded, “Please give us a hand…🥺!” The Sué family had sent a letter that said, “We expect that you side with the Sués.” 

Just when the Mōris’ fort was about to crumble, 200 Murakami warships showed up... and BEAT THE SH** OUT of the Sué family 😂.

Just 2 years after their tremendous and unexpected loss, the Sué family was wiped out from the face of Japan by the Mōri family. 

Sincerity counts 😁!

Viewed We were so close to a really fire Tekken after TWT ended. 

The pros started showing tons of counterplay and creative solutions. At the STL Finals, Knee used Snake Edge to beat a Yoshimitsu Bad Breath!!

At Korea vs. Pakistan, we saw tons of Heat Bursts get sidestepped and launched. 

And who can forget how hype Numan vs. Edge was at TWT 2024. 

A few nerfs to the homing strings, the tracking heat bursts, and the chip damage would have put the game in an amazing state. 

For new moves, the Heat Smash adjustments I generally enjoy a lot. The Heat Smashes reintroduced as Meter moves are generally not my favorite, including Lili and Steve's. But these weakness cover-ups and do-everything moves feel like a modded game, not a mainline title update. 

At the end of Season 1, I was logging on every day to drill Tekken and rewire myself to learn to attack better. I was running long sets with my friends, streaming to entertain and educate, and always looking forward to logging on again. 

Now, I have to decide if the new vision of Tekken is worth completely rewriting again for. The new rank system is really cool to me. But the gameplay required to climb it, personally, is not for me. 

I was on a battle high of reading and studying the patch while trying to make balanced, level-headed content about it. 

Now that I'm coming down from it, morale is pretty low. 

I don't think my opinion holds much weight to the development team, but I wouldn't have made nearly daily videos this whole year if I didn't love Tekken. I wanted to share and teach what makes the series so special. I don't know if I will have the passion for that in this new direction. 

Please revert the patch.

Viewed Neighbor problems existed since neighbors existed. Here’s a Japanese folktale 

Once upon a time there was a greedy rich man and a poor man living beside each other with a fence in between.

Every spring, the poor man looked forward to drinking sake under the big cherry blossom tree that grew in his yard. Meanwhile, the rich man wasn’t happy about lacking a tree of his own.

So when some branches grew into the rich man’s side of the fence, he secretly tied a rope to one and pulled it towards his house. 

By the next spring, the tree had bent so much that most of the flowers bloomed on the rich man’s side of the fence. He invited people to come see the flowers and charged visitors an entrance fee. 

The poor man was furious about his neighbor making money from his own tree, and complained. But the reply was, “Flowers growing on my side are mine. I can do whatever I please.”

So one day, the poor man started playing festive music loudly. It sounded so fun that the greedy rich man had to stick his head into a hole in the fence to look. 

Then, the poor man grabbed the rich man’s nose and twisted it 90 degrees 👃. In Japanese, “flower” and “nose” are homonyms 😆.

The rich man apologized and pushed back the branch of the cherry blossom tree. By the time the branch was back on the poor man’s side, the bent nose had also moved back into place ☺️.

The story is called “Kakigoshi no Hana to Hana.”

Painting by UTAGAWA Hiroshige (1797 - 1858).

Viewed Inō Tadataka was the first man to make an accurate map of Japan in 1821 by circumambulating the entire country on foot 😆. 

The results of his 17-year project and his takeaway from the journey, I think, is relevant to many of us.

Tadataka got into studying during his youth, and dreamt of becoming a scholar one day. But at 17, he was married off into a family running a slumping saké brewery, and his first challenge was to learn the business and turn it around. He did.

At 36, he became the mayor of his village, and his second challenge was to help his people overcome a major famine that killed 900,000 people nationwide. He did, and his village lost no one to hunger.

At 50, he succeeded the house to his son, but was not done with life. 

Instead of retiring, he moved to Tokyo (then called Edo City) to learn astronomy under a teacher 19 years younger than he was. 

He came to wonder, “How big is the Earth, really?” And to find out, he needed to survey the Japanese islands with precision.

So at 56, he trekked around the huge Hokkaido island in the north (which was largely unknown even to the Japanese government) and created a map so detailed that he was commissioned to do the same for the whole country. He did. 

After 17 years of walking, his map came out to be just as accurate as what we now see on Google Maps 😎. 

Before his death at 74, he left these words: “Keep walking, because that’s what’s important.”

Persistence is key, no matter your trade!

While the dominant, light-pink and flamboyant Somei Yoshino breed (the kind you would typically see in photos of the Japanese spring) blooms in late March and lasts only for a week, 

Kawazu Zakura blooms in February and lasts for nearly a month. 

Yaezakura blooms a week or two after Somei Yoshino, pleasing the eyes of passersby with their over-20 petals per flower as opposed to the 5 petaled Somei Yoshino. 

The Former Nakagawa Waterfront Park in Tokyo has a riverside walkway with 9 breeds of cherry blossom trees, from early bloomers to laters ones, ensuring there is some pink above your head throughout spring ☺️.

Perhaps it’s a small example of how fighting the urge to favor a certain species over various others can benefit us all ✨.

Viewed Noh masks are spooky because:

1. Almost none of them represent humans. They’re mostly ghosts or goblins with serious resentments, so you shouldn’t expect to run into many smiley faces in Noh theater. 

2. Their expressions are made so that they can be interpreted in a variety of ways. The same face will look mad, sad or excited depending on the angle the actor faces, the gestures made by the actor, and the lighting of the stage. 

So without those contexts, the faces look alien—you can’t read the content of their minds because they are yet to express any emotion fully. 

Noh mask photography is a niche but hot hobby for some - they say what’s interesting is how the message expressed through the photos vary by the angle the mask is shot. 

To give you away a secret, these masks are subtly asymmetrical, just like our faces, and therefore provide photographers the joy of finding their best angles, just like how some of us have found our best selfie angles.

Viewed Niiro Tadamoto was an unstoppable samurai commander who was nicknamed “Thumb-finger Musashi” as his middle name was Musashi and he was always first when counting the biggest contributors in every battle. 

But Tadamoto wasn’t just a fierce warrior but an avid poet, and a generally compassionate guy.

In 1581, Tadamoto surrounded Minamata Castle from land and sea as part of a project to conquer enemy territory.

Tadamoto wanted to urge the opponent to surrender. So he wrote half a verse on a letter and tied it to an arrow, which he shot into the enemy castle. It read:

秋風に 皆また落つる 木の葉かな
You won’t want your soldiers to fall as leaves do after an autumn wind.

Japanese poems consisted of a first and second half, so leaving the second half unwritten signified a call for a reply. He found out there was a poetry-savvy samurai on the defending side, too, as a reply came back tied to an arrow. It said:

寄せては沈む 月の浦波
Or you can beautifully surge and then break on our castle walls like waves do on a moonlit shore.

The opponent held up for a while but unluckily for them, the news was brought that their HQ had fallen. They surrendered to Tadamori.

Another poem Tadamoto is remembered by is an elegy for his late wife. He lived until 85, and his son and even grandchildren died before he did. The poem goes:

さぞな春 つれなき老いと 思ふらむ
今年も花の のちに残れば
Spring would think I’m an old man without grace.

Viewed Of the 27 kids a Shogun had, 26 died before they became 13, and 18 died before the age of 1. The cause was not a plague or a curse, but sadly, makeup. 

The child mortality rate was tremendously high in 19th-century Japan: almost half of all births resulted in the death of the child way before puberty. But the 96% premature mortality rate of the 12th Shogun, Tokugawa Ieyoshi’s children was on another level. 

His father’s reign was characterized by luxury, art, and fashion. People dressed in ornate clothes and put on lavish makeup, adhering powder all over the body—the white-skinned look had become a trend among the eight wives of Ieyoshi and even their ladies-in-waiting, too.

They would puff powder onto their faces, necks, and breasts, and then breastfed the many children of the Shogun. Little did they know that their powders included lead and mercury, or how harmful those substances were to the human body.

The babies were drinking from breasts coated in poison. 

The only child who survived past puberty was Ieyoshi’s heir, Iesada, who also only lived to be 35. He also showed signs of brain damage and a speech impediment.

Viewed “Hmm, it must suck to be unblind 😂” said Hanawa Hokiichi, a blind man who turned himself into a nationally respected scholar in 18th-century Japan when audiobooks didn’t even exist!

Hokiichi lost his eyesight at age 7, and his mom died when he was 11 😢. But he was not very bummed out about life. When he heard about how blind people made a living reciting literature, he thought, “If someone can support a family by memorizing a mere 40-volume book, I guess life’s not as hard as people say it is 😏.” He moved to Edo (the old name of Tokyo).

There, he learned the standard skills of the optically challenged—music, massage, and acupuncture. But he had no talent in any of them. 

He found joy in listening to the books his few customers read out loud for him while he gave them a bad massage. Hokiichi made up his mind to live as a scholar. 

He memorized all the lectures he listened to in one go. 

To give you an idea of how his brain worked: 
At the end bit of his life, Hokiichi attended a poetry reading get-together. After he got home, he tried to recite the 50 poems, each of which he heard just once, and said, “Oh, I can’t recall 3. I think I’m dying 😞.” Hokiichi eventually spent 40 years compiling an encyclopedia of 666 volumes and became a legend. 

One night, when Hokiichi was giving a lecture to his students, a gust of wind blew out all the candles, and the classroom became pitch-dark. Hokiichi was unaffected, but everyone panicked as they couldn’t take notes. “Hmm, it must suck to be unblind 😂.” He died in 1821.

In 1937, an American woman came all the way to Japan to caress the worn desk the blind legend used. Helen Keller said she could feel the warm personality of Hokiichi, of whom she was the biggest fan 🥹.

Viewed The stereotypical personality traits of women of Aomori, the second northernmost and super snowy prefecture of Japan, is that they are initiative takers. 

Aomori is the third biggest hotspot of female business owners in Japan. It's also said that women of Aomori are decisive, stubborn, and tend to make the first move while men tend to be shy and reactive 😁. 

We're not sure if Princess Oura of the Ōura samurai family in western Aomori made the first move, but in 1563, she met a boy who came to live in her castle as a refugee. 

They were both 14, and surprisingly, in a time when marriage of convenience was the norm in samurai families, the two wed at 18. The boy was renamed Ōura Tamenobu.

The Ōura couple led the family to a wild success. Tamenobu was an ambitious man who conspired to break the Ōuras free from the rule of their boss, the Nanbu samurai family. 

And Princess Oura was very hands-on in helping Tamenobu materialize his vision. Before a battle, Princess Oura kicked the castle door open (figuratively) and distributed rice balls to the soldiers herself 🍙. 

When a messenger reported that the Nanbu family was making headway and Tamenobu's men had run out of bullets, Princess Oura ordered her servants to gather all the tin-made items in the castle, melt them to forge new bullets, and had the products delivered to the front line 🔫.

Thanks to his sharp wife, Tamenobu won the battle and drove away the Nanbu family from western Aomori. 

Their castle never went under attack, and we can still visit it today and see it standing the way it was some 400 years ago. 

Ōura Castle was renamed Hirosaki Castle in 1627 by Tamenobu's son, and is now an Important Cultural Heritage.

Viewed Aoto Fujitsuna was a samurai in the 13th century who was remembered as a regional governor of unmatched generosity. 

It’s said that he would distribute much of his salary to the poor living in the region he governed. Whenever and wherever Fujitsuna was in charge, corruption of public officers dwindled and peasants behaved. 

Here’s a folk tale that gives us an idea of how people viewed him ☺️:

One night, Fujitsuna dropped a 10-mon coin in the river he was crossing. He had his servants search for it in the water, but it was too dark.

“Do we have a torch?”
“No, sir. It’s sold at the store over there but it costs 50-mon.”
“A llright, can you go buy one?”
“But sir… Math 😫!!”
“It’s okay. Just go buy it.”

With the torch, Fujitsuka and his men found the 10-mon coin but onlookers made fun of them behind their backs. 
Hearing what had happened, Fujitsuna’s samurai friend laughed at him. 

But Fujitsuna smiled and said, “The 10-mon I dropped in the water would have been a 10-mon lost from the economy forever. It’s back in the game now, and a local merchant earned 50-mon. All is well ☺️.”

What people with the bigger picture do 😁.

Viewed During the 140 years of nation-wide samurai battle royale called the Sengoku Period (1467 - 1603), Katana swords were only the 5th deadliest weapon.

Here’s a list of the biggest causes of death in battle, ranked in the order of deadliness:

1. Matchlock rifle
2. Bow and arrow
3. Spear
4. Rocks
5. Katana sword

Rocks were thrown whenever and wherever they were available and dealt serious damage. They could kill you instantly or blind you depending on where they hit. Scary 😫!

Many died from infections caused by injuries from bullets and arrows. Army surgeons would carry around herbs and solutions they would rub onto wounds to stop them from bleeding. 

But in the absence of a proper surgeon, the most dreadful makeshift remedies were practiced. 

Seeing you bleeding badly, a fellow soldier may rub any of the following items onto your wound:

1. Common grass
2. Salt
3. Soy sauce
4. Egg white
5. Horse poop
6. Soldier poop

Salt was actually rubbed on wounds 😩!!! The pain was likely worse than the injury itself.  

If the pain didn’t shock you to death, next came severe inflammation caused by a bacterial infection, to which the lay surgeon may have exclaimed, “Those enemies… They must have shot you with a poison arrow 😠!!” 

So I’d like to revise the list of deadly weapons to:

1. Matchlock rifle 
2. Bow and arrow
3. Goodwill without science
4. Spear
5. Rocks

So Katana swords don’t even make it to the list 😂.

Viewed The samurai statue in the Imperial Palace Gardens is of Kusunoki Masashige, the symbol of unyielding loyalty… and also, I think a reminder for people in power to listen to their staff 😂.

By the 14th century, Japan was ruled not by the emperor, but in effect, by a samurai government that had gained far greater power. The emperor was just there as window dressing. 

Throwing a tantrum to the situation, Emperor Go-daigo initiated an uprising against the samurai government. 

As a royalty, Go-daigo was adept in poetry, but not in warfare, so his battles didn’t go very well. 

It’s said that one night, he dreamed about himself looking for his seat at a party. He was told by a mysterious boy that his seat shall be found under a tree extending its branch toward the south. 

Tree… 木.
South… 南.

“Go find someone who has the character 楠 in his name!” Go-daigo told his servants, and that was the enlightening reason an indie samurai called Kusunoki Masashige 楠木正成 was hired, out of the blue, to help Go-daigo realize his ambition 😂. Ancient people took dreams seriously.

Masashige, although puzzled, swore allegiance. 

Masashige brought strategies and tactics to Go-daigo’s initiative. He turned the war around and the samurai government was defeated. 

But Go-daigo privileged nobles too much under his new government, and a talented samurai called Ashikaga Takauji revolted and raised an army. 

Masashige knew how great a warlord Takauji was, so he proposed that they draw Takauji to their side. Go-daigo refused. 

When Takauji attacked, Masashige proposed that Go-daigo retreat from the capital once because there was no chance of winning. Go-daigo refused because that would be embarrassing. And lost 😂.

Masashige still fought for his boss and died 😢. Go-daigo was kicked out of the capital and a new samurai government was established.

…Leave it to the pros 😩!!!

Viewed A faithful husband but a psychopath. A psychopath but a faithful husband—words that best describe Hosokawa Tadaoki (1563 - 1646).

Tadaoki was a high-performing feudal lord who was married to a most beautiful princess, Akechi Tama. The couple was in a strained relationship due to Tadaoki’s hyper-possessive approach to love. 

One day, the couple was having a meal while several gardeners were at work. Tadaoki, Tama, and three gardeners were conversing happily until Tadaoki suddenly spat sternly at one of them, “What are you looking at?” 

“Nothing, sir.”
“You were looking at Tama.”
“No, I wasn’t, sir.”
“You were looking at my beloved wife!!!”

Tadaoki rose to his feet, fast-walked towards the gardener, drew his sword, and killed the poor guy in one swing. He came back to the dinner table and wiped the blood off his sword with Tama’s kimono. 

Tama did not approve of her husband’s cruelty and continued to wear the bloody kimono for days. 

The sword owned by Tadaoki became known as Kasen-Kanesada, named after the blacksmith Kanesada and as a satire of Tadaoki’s madness—drawing a parallel between the 36 immortalized poets of the past (the 36 Kasens) and the 36 servants he had slain 😩.

Tama sought spiritual refuge in Catholicism and was secretly baptized, hence renamed Hosokawa Gracia. Tadaoki was furious upon discovering her conversion. But he could not force her to renounce her faith as Gracia was adamant, and after all, Tadaoki loved her, despite in a twisted manner.

Although Gracia’s new faith did help her regain vigor, ironically, it didn’t allow her to divorce her husband. 

Ultimately, when a political enemy tried to take her hostage, Gracia decided to turn the event into a sad opportunity to take her own life. As Catholicism does not approve of suicide, she had a servant kill her to put an end to her tangled life 🥺.

When war broke out against the very enemy who triggered Gracia’s death, Tadaoki fought with tremendous fury and contributed greatly to victory. He gave Gracia a Catholic funeral. 

Hosokawa Gracia is the model of Mariko in the novel and drama, SHOGUN.

Viewed The wrong hire will kill your business.

Here’s what 1000+ taught me about attracting and retaining talent:

Clarity vs. Performance

You owe your employees clarity, they owe you performance.

Clearly communicate expectations to your team. Be specific about goals and success metrics.

In return, hold employees accountable for results.

Create An Environment For Success

Your job is to create fertile soil for talent to thrive. It's their job to grow.

Enable success by providing resources and support. Set them up to win.

But remember, you can't force growth. Focus on enablement, not ensurement.

Clear KPIs

Set clear expectations with KPIs tied to company goals.

KPIs show employees what success looks like in their role.

They remove ambiguity and emotion from performance evaluations. 

KPIs are your north star.

Promoting from Within

Promoting from within boosts morale. Employees see hard work rewarded.

But never compromise on talent. Putting the wrong person in a role hurts everyone.

Promote when you can, but prioritize putting the right people in the right places.

Hire Doers

You need people who can roll up their sleeves and do the work.

Look for:
• Willingness to get in the trenches
• Comfort with ambiguity

Build a team that leads by example.

Viewed The wisest man of our lifetime:
Naval Ravikant.

He co-founded AngelList and was an early investor in Polymarket, Notion, and Uber.

And he famously said: “Earn with your mind, not your time.”

Here’s his philosophy on getting rich without getting lucky: 

Ownership Is The Only Path To Wealth

“If you don't own a piece of a business, you don't have a path towards financial freedom.” 

Just look at the world’s top CEOs (base salary vs. net worth):
• Tim Cook ($3M vs $2.2B)
• Jamie Diamond ($1.5M vs $2.8B)

Ownership > income.

Play The Long Game

"Play long-term games with long-term people." 

Short-term people think in days & months.

Long-term people think in years & decades.

Time reveals who's actually winning.

Leverage Is A Force Multiplier

“It doesn’t take money to make money, it takes leverage to make money.”

Everyone sees the obvious levers: code, content, capital.

But the hidden lever is judgment - knowing which lever to pull.

Poor judgment turns leverage into a weapon against yourself.

Obsess Over High-Value Skills

“Learn to sell, learn to build. If you can do both, you will be unstoppable.”

Become addicted to learning how to: 
• Create undeniable value
• Make that value obvious to the world

One skill makes you valuable. Both skills make you wealthy.

Extreme Ownership

“Embrace accountability and take business risks under your own name.”

Most founders hide behind brands and corporations.

But the real power comes from putting yourself on the line. Own every outcome.

Every win and loss adds to your story.

Avoid Business Advice

“There is no skill called ‘business.’ Avoid business magazines and business classes.”

The secret of business isn't locked in an MBA program.

It's in understanding how things actually work:
• Identifying a known problem
• Building a solution people rave about
• Knowing your customers better than they know themselves

Compound Interest = Everything

"All the benefits in life come from compound interest - relationship, money, habits - anything of importance."

Warren Buffett made 99% of his wealth after age 65. People quit too early because they underestimate the power of time.

The real gains start in year 15, not year 1.

True Test Of Intelligence

“The only true test of intelligence is if you get what you want out of life.”

Goals make demands.

They force you to become the person who can achieve them. 

Are you prepared to pay the price your goals demand?

Viewed A 14th-century Japanese hermit left with us an idea that’s both peculiar and worth incorporating in our modern-day lives. 

Kenkō was a Buddhist monk who fast-tracked his life to become a hermit as early as in his late 20s. He lived a carefree life alone, taking long walks, writing poetry, and above all, documenting his trail of thoughts in an essay for nearly two decades. 

Likely because Kenkō avidly engaged in people-watching through mingling among all social classes, much of the life advice he gives through this essay makes strong cases.

One of which is his idea regarding the use of space in your home. The state of your living space represents the construct of the resident’s mind, he thought.

The residence of a certain wealthy man screamed wealth and perfection; as a guest, he felt as if he were being suffocated with a bombardment of information. 

But the residence of another wealthy man compelled him to relax and have a genuinely good time. In the man’s house was a little space with an ambiguous purpose. 

It was populated with items without a place to be, as if it were a space in his mind for half-thoughts and pebbles of ideas, waiting to be completed with ideas a guest, like Kenkō, might bring in. 

He always had most delightful conversations with the host ☺️. 

Photos at Edo-Tokyo Open Air Architectural Museum. I recommend a visit!

Viewed The biggest mistake I had been making as a Tokyo citizen until I became a Japanese culture enthusiast was thinking that, ‘Having fun in Tokyo requires money.’

The truth was the exact opposite. You just have to know the flower calendar to enjoy the way Tokyo has been designed to be enjoyed since 400 years ago. 

So again this year, here’s my destination cheat sheet that will come in handy if you happen to be in Tokyo in spring. 

Mid-February - Mid March
Go see plum blossoms at:
- Ikegami Baien (Japanese garden)
- Imperial Garden (Huge Japanese garden)
- Yushima Tenmangū (Shrine)
- Koishikawa Kōrakuen (Huge Japanese garden)
- Kameido Tenjin (Shrine)
- Mukōjima Hyakkaen (Japanese garden)
- Takao Baigō (Mountain full of plums)

Late March - Early April
Go see cherry blossoms at:
- Rikugien (Japanese garden)
- Shinjuku Gyoen (Huge Japanese garden)
- Omokagebashi (Bridge immersed in cherry blossoms)
- Sakurazaka (Slope immersed in cherry blossoms)
- Nishi Yōga Dōri (Road endlessly immersed in cherry blossoms)
- Meguro River (River immersed in cherry blossoms)
- Tachikawa Kōen Negawa Ryokudō (Another such river)
- Showa Kinen Park (Mammoth park with cherry blossoms everywhere)
- Kanda Myōjin (Shrine)

Late April to early May 
Go see azalea at:
- Nezu Shrine
- Komagome Station
- Shinjuku Gyoen 
- Shiobune Kannonji (Temple with a hill full of azalea)

Many more but that’s all the space I have! All these places are admission free, or costs peanuts to see. The best of Tokyo!

Viewed Continuation of the story of Otokichi, an average Japanese sailor who was cast away by a storm and finally naturalized as an Englishman in the 19th century. 

After circling the globe over a course of 5 long years, Otokichi was finally on board the Morrison, an American ship bound for home—Japan.

The Morrison caught sight of Edo Bay (now called Tokyo Bay) in 1837.

…But to the crew’s dismay, the coastal guards started firing canons at the Morrison and wouldn’t stop. Japan had issued the Edict to Repel Foreign Vessels a few years back and coastal guards were to fire at foreign ships (Dutch and Chinese ships were OK), no questions asked. 

The Morrison was an unarmed merchant ship meaning to do no harm. It had to turn around and head back out to sea. 

They did manage to stop by another port in the southern-most tip of Kyushu Island where the samurai clan there was a bit more open-minded. 

Though the Morrison was able to get supplies, their offer to return Otokichi was rejected. Japan’s isolation policy did not even allow Japanese nationals who had left the country to return 🥺. 

Looking at Otokichi’s footprints in history after the unthinkable rejection, he seemed to have made up his mind about his new identity. 

Otokichi got a job at a British firm in Shanghai. He married a British colleague named Marry and had a daughter. 

He came to Japan as a translator on a British ship in 1849 but disguised himself as a Chinese and did not land.

Otokichi helped other Japanese castaways board a Chinese ship so they could return to Japan, but he himself didn’t.

He came to Japan as a translator again in 1854 and was offered a position at the port of Nagasaki. He politely declined.

After moving to Singapore, Otokichi naturalized as a British citizen and named himself John Matthew Ottoson. 

His son John W. Ottoson moved to Japan and naturalized there. He renamed himself Otokichi, and buried half of his father’s remains in his hometown. 

The other half remains in Singapore 😌🥹.

Viewed There was an average-Joe 19th-century sailor who was cast away to America due to a storm, never got to return to Japan again but became the first Japanese person to become an Englishman 🇯🇵🇬🇧. 

Learning about his life story will help us realize the petiteness of our own problems 😂.

Otokichi was a regular sailor doing a regular old job on a regular old domestic route in Japan. But one day in 1832, the ship got washed away by a storm, drifted on the Pacific Ocean for 14 months, and was cast ashore on the Olympic Peninsula of what is now the state of Washington. 

He was rescued by a local Native American tribe… and was quickly trained to be their slave 😫. Then, he was sold off to an English fleet. 

The English decided to help Otokichi return to Japan, so they brought him over to London once. Otokichi was allowed to tour London for a day, and so he became the first Japanese person to set foot in England.

He went on board a ship bound for Macau in 1835. Apparently, Otokichi had learned the English language by then and was asked to help translate the Bible. He did it.

In Macau, Otokichi joined several other Japanese castaways and together boarded an American merchant ship, the Morrison, bound for Edo City, the capital of samurai-ruled Japan. 

Japan had not traded with any Western country except the Netherlands due to their 200-year-long isolation policy, but the Morrison thought that Japn would trade with America if it helped these poor Japanese sailors come home. 

“Finally, finally, I will return after encircling the globe 🥺!!” thought Otokichi…

But never had he imagined the shores of Japan would reject him so utterly.

Viewed A Noh theater play is about a poor man who sacrifices his cute little Bonsai trees to fire to warm the house for a stranger who needed shelter in snowy winter.

In the play “Hachinoki,” Sano Tsuneyo is an unlucky samurai who had lost his territory to a relative who embezzled it. One snowy night, he invites a traveling monk to stay for a night at his house. 

As he tells how he tumbled down the samurai hierarchy, he runs out of firewood. Worried his guest would be cold, Tsuneyo takes out his plum, cherry and pine Bonsai trees—his proud collection he had grown with care—and throws them into the fire. 

He kept his now-rusty armor and spear in a corner of his house, waiting for the day the shogun summons him on the battlefield. The monk thanked him and left.

Spring came and all samurai, rich or poor, were summoned to fight for the shogun. A man in rusty armor with a rusty spear, appeared on a skinny horse, and joined the march. It was Tsuneyo.

Tsuneyo was called in front of the regent to the shogun, Hōjō Tokiyori. Tokiyori confessed he was the traveling monk Tsuneyo had helped on that snowy night. 

“I visited you in disguise. I’m glad to see you keep to your promise you made that night.”

Tokiyori gave the territory Tsuneyo had lost, and as a bonus, bestowed three more plots of land named after the three Bonsai trees he gave up: 

梅田 Umeda (Plum-fields)
桜井 Sakurai (Cherry-well)
松井田 Matsuida (Pine-well-fields)

I’d be touched by Tsuneyo’s actions, too 🥹.

Viewed Kyoto and Osaka (western Japan) used to be the political and economic center of Japan respectively for 1,100 years, until Tokyo (called Edo before) grew into a megalopolis.

Western Japan had a huge head start in cultivating food culture, and therefore was where all the most seasoned sake breweries were. Food also generally tastes more sophisticated there still now, in my opinion 😋. 

So in the early days of Edo’s growth, the city relied heavily on food/beverage produced and transported from western Japan. They just tasted better. 

But then at one point, people realized that sake was more flavorful after being brought to Edo, than in Western Japan where the sake was made. 

The reason was: sake got swirled on the cargo ships to Edo, and by the time they arrived, they tasted milder and acquired the fragrance of the wooden barrels they were swirling in. These traveling sake came to be called “富士見酒 Fuji-mi zake” because it passed by Mt. Fuji on their route to Edo 🗻.

So this beautiful woman may have had a bit too much sake the day she was drawn by Hokusai.

Viewed 550 years back, Ōta Dōkan was an ace samurai serving for an established samurai family that ruled a region that is now a part of Tokyo. 

He was smart as a whip and loyal as Hachi the idolized dog of Shibuya station. 

He won over 30 consecutive battles, built two invincible castles (one of which eventually became the emperor’s residence 500 years later) and resolved a civil war caused by an offspring of his master, Uesugi Sadamasa, all for the sake of fulfilling his role as a vassal. 

It was clear to anyone that Dōkan was the one keeping the world go round, and his master Sadamasa feared that he might eventually be overthrown by this overly talented subordinate. 

One day, Dōkan was invited to Sadamasa’s house and was told to take a bath to relax. When he came out of the bath (unarmed in every way)… an assassin was awaiting. 

Knowing that Dōkan also excelled in poetry, the assassin challenged him to a poetry improvisation, initiating the first half of a two-part poem: 

— かかる時 さこそ命の 惜しからめ
How dreadful it must be to lose a life full of accomplishments

Doukan responded with an answer poem:

— かねてなき身と 思ひ知らずば
Only that I have considered myself dead long ago. 

He had already accepted his likely samurai-fate of early death. Meanwhile, after getting rid of Doukan, his master Sadamasa repeated war aimlessly and his family was soon defeated by another up-and-rising warlord.

Ōta Doukan is remembered as a legendary samurai, while Sadamasa’s name is hardly recalled. 

The restoration of Nezu Shrine was one of Doukan’s many successful projects, and is still there in Tokyo, now designated a national cultural heritage.

Viewed Sleep is the most common thing I get asked about. People want good sleep, and try to get good sleep, but are frustrated by the difficulty.  

Sleep is the most powerful drug available.  For performance, mental health and well-being.

After years of experiencing the same challenges, I figured out how to reliably get high quality rest.  I achieve the best sleep score in the world. Eight months of perfect 100% sleep. 

Here is how you do it: 

1. Build your life around sleep - right now sleep is an afterthought in culture. When you're done watching your movie...when you're finished with work..when you feel like it. You need to treat sleep with the same level of seriousness and devotion as you do your work. It demands your best performance. 

2. Consume your final meal at least two hours before bed - if your bedtime is 10 pm, finish eating by 8 pm. Then day by day, move back 30 minutes. So by the end of the first week, you're having your final meal of the day around 5 pm. Do this to lower your resting heart rate. You're giving your body time to digest food and prepare for sleep. The lower your resting heart rate the better your sleep. 

You're going to feel a little hungry, that's ok. It's a good thing. Soon you'll learn to love the feeling because of how good you'll feel in the morning. Work through the discomfort. 

3. Avoid blue light before bed - an hour or two before bed, try to avoid blue light. That means off screens (or eliminate blue light from your screens, there are apps and settings to do this on computer and mobile devices). Instead, turn on red and amber lights. Light can significantly affect your readiness to fall asleep. 

4. Consistency - the body loves routine and will reward you with powerful sleep performance. Go to bed +/- 30 minutes of your chosen bedtime every single day. Create the habit and stay with the habit. 

4. Create a wind down routine  - you can't just finish work and put your head on the pillow and expect great sleep. You need to calm your body and mind down. You need separation from work. Read a book, go for a walk, do a breathing exercise, take a bath, meditate, and journal.

I have a routine where I maintain an internal dialog, breaking myself out into various characters "Ambitious Bryan" "Anxious Bryan" etc. and I allow them to tell me about all the pressing things on their mind. I write them down and tell them that I hear them and will address them tomorrow after we get a great night's sleep. Viewed The economic landscape has changed so dramatically in the last 50 years, that if you're running the old “American Dream” play book, you’ll end up worse off than you started.

It no longer makes no sense to:
- Go to college on debt
- Get a regular job and save
- Focus on buying a house for your nest egg

America is now the world’s largest debtor.

We have spent WAY more than we take in from tax revenue, and we’ve used money printing to pay for a litany of mistakes (the 2008 financial crisis & forever wars most egregiously).

This monetary policy has created inflation, and inflation pushes people to save money, and effectively forces everyone to gamble in order to just keep up. Your money is literally worth less year after year.

Because of that, if you want to get ahead, here’s the new playbook:

1. Avoid debt, even if that means using YouTube and books to educate yourself.

2. Be far more critical of real estate. It’s not guaranteed to be bad, but large corporations like Black Rock are driving prices up because they are using real estate as a place to put their money to work, to beat inflation.

3. Minimize risk, but make sure your money is earning a high enough return to keep up with inflation.

4. Invest on a long time horizon.

5. Follow Ray Dalio’s advice, and find 12-15 uncorrelated streams of investment income.

6. Do NOT despair, and do not YOLO everything you own into any one thing. Not crypto. Not meme stocks. Not anything. Despite what people may tell you, wise diversification will help you avoid calamity.

7. Spend less than you make.

8. Use geography to find tax advantaged locations with a reasonable cost of living.

9. Outperform your peers at work. If you can make people money, you’ll always be paid well.

If all of this sounds like a headache, it is.

And the fact that you have to do this to not have your savings eroded by inflation is exactly why you should be mad, and why you should learn about how money really works.

Keep your wits about you.

Focus on skill acquisition, and remember, while the game is most certainly rigged, it’s still winnable.

Viewed Checking to see if the drapes are hung is a quick and easy way to tell if a traditional Japanese restaurant is open for business. But the drapes coming to be understood as “We are open” signs was unintended.

The earliest sighting of shop-front drapes, or ‘noren,’ dates back to the 1100s; it was just a tool to block the blazing sunlight and dusty wind from coming inside. 

But by the 1300s, people realized the ad space noren could provide, and shops began adorning their noren with emblems. The literacy rate was generally low then, and designed shapes were the most effective means to raise the awareness of each business. 

So the understanding that a shop is open emerged gradually and naturally as  shopkeepers would hang their noren at the door at the start of business hours and take them down at the end.

Because some customers would wipe their hands on the noren as they left, at one point, worn norens were indicators of successful businesses.

Long ago, there were two brothers living together. The elder one was greedy and lazy; he made the younger one work in the fields while he sat around at home.

One day the younger one got married, and it was time to move out, but his brother refused to share even a spec of the rice field he had inherited. So the couple tried to cultivate a wasteland, but they didn’t make a single grain of rice that year. 

It was New Year’s Eve, and the younger one asked his brother to spare them some food, but he was driven away.

But on his way home, an old man gave him a stone mortar. He said, “If you turn the mortar to the right, it will produce whatever you wish for, and if you turn it to the left, it will stop.”

When he got home, the younger one tried the gadget out, and indeed, out came rice, salmon, horses, and a spacious manor…the couple became a billionaire overnight. They invited everyone in the village over to celebrate the New Year together.

The elder one, not liking what had happened a single bit, caught sight of the couple churning out dessert for the guests out of the mortar. So that night, he stole the magic tool along with the freshly generated dessert, and got on a boat to leave the village his ancestors had lived forever. 

Offshore, the elder one was craving for something salty after eating up everyone’s dessert. So he wished for salt and turned the mortar to the right.

Out came a flood of salt…but he didn’t know how to stop it 😱.

The boat sank from the weight of the salt, along with the elder brother and the mortar. 

The mortar pumps salt at the bottom of the sea, still now, and that is why the sea tastes the way it does.

The story is called “Shio fuki usu.”

Viewed What’s with Japan’s obsession with red and white? It’s the color combination of the uniform of shrine maidens, Japan’s all-time favorite bird, the crane, and of course, the Japanese flag. 

The Japanese people have lost track of the reason the combination came to be favored. When we realized, we were already putting red pickled plums on white rice; brides had already been wearing all white and reddened rice (called Sekihan) had been served on wedding days. 

The color red is considered to be lucky in neighboring China, and the Chinese cultural influence Japan received over 1000 years ago is likely to have affected our view of the color. 

Also, red is the color of life—babies, the sun, blood. White was associated with purity and death. White was worn at funerals and by the deceased, to make sure he/she could travel to heaven pure and clean. A theory for the preference for red and white is that they represent life and death simultaneously. 

But having read extensively about the lives of peasants in Japanese history, I think the festive feel of red and white is derived also from the people’s cultural memory. 

For hundreds of years, peasants could often not afford to eat refined white rice and instead ate unrefined brown grains all year. It was only on special occasions like New Year’s and days of festivals when they could eat abundant white rice and white rice cakes. And what was the most lively color that complimented white? Red 😁! 

Red and white were the colors that separated daily life and festive days. Culture is a result of the complex intertwining of history, lifestyle, and feelings experienced across generations.

Viewed Japanese warlords fought on the battlefield fair and square for honor and glory… well, maybe for glory but not always for honor, and definitely not fair and square 😂. 

Though a son of a blacksmith, Kato Kiyomasa thrived in the late 16th century as a fearless warlord, often entrusted the front line. He was recruited into the team of the would-be ruler of Japan, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, for being a distant relative. 

Just like his employer, not having grown up in a samurai family may have given him an edge. His goal as a warlord was to help the Toyotomi regime prosper, not die an honorable death in battle—a fate most samurai were taught to aspire to. 

So it was in 1589 that Kiyomasa left one of his unique legacies. Rebels to the Toyotomi regime rose in arms at Shiki Castle, located in what is now Kumamoto Prefecture. Kiyomasa led his troops to reinforce his ally who was unexpectedly being pushed back by the rebels.

An enemy warlord, Kiyama Danjō, despite leading troops just a third of the size of Kiyomasa’s, came charging in ferociously. Seeing the way the melee was going, it looked like there was a slight chance Kiyomasa’s troops would bend to the enemy’s momentum. 

Furthermore, Danjō challenged Kiyomasa on a 1-on-1 to increase his chances of winning. Danjō was famed for his skills with the bow and arrow—not a favorable opponent for Kiyomasa, a master spearsman. 

So Kiyomasa dropped his spear to the ground and drew his sword. “One-on-ones are meant to be fought fair and square, with the sword, don’t you think?” he called out, to which Danjō agreed, came near and drew his sword. 

Then, Kiyomasa, in a blink of an eye, picked up the spear he had just introduced to gravity and stabbed Danjō to death.

The spectators may have been like, “Bro… 😩,” but victory was victory! The rebellion was extinguished soon after, thanks to Kiyomasa’s I-play-for-keeps-not-for-fun mindset… 😂

Viewed Santa Claus made his first arrival in Japan in 1900. But to be accurate, his name was 三太九郎 Santa Kurō, not Santa Claus 😂.

Likely in an attempt to make a more relatable first impression, the publisher that published the first storybook about Santa transliterated his name into Kanji. Reindeers were not known to Japan yet so a donkey seems to have substituted them. 

We can imagine the Japanese illustrator, with his limited knowledge of Western traditions and aesthetics, did his best to depict Santa, and the end result was a mailman dressed like a caped Moses 😂😂😂. 

The story is set in Japan and is about Santa Kurō dropping off a present beside the futon of a boy in a struggling family. The narrative carries a blend of the serious vibe of the previous samurai-age and a militaristic feel of the upcoming wartime Japan; it ends, word for word, with these phrases:

“Christmas Banzai! Nichiyou Gakkou (Sunday school) Banzai!”
“Santa Kurō Banzai! Santa Kurō Banzai!!!” 

Things were taken absolutely seriously a century ago 😂😂😂.

Here’s to 124 years of Japan’s love for Santa Claus. Merry Christmas 🥂!

Viewed Kyōgen are traditional comedic theater performances that are typically coupled with the more serious Noh theater plays, both still going strong with over 650 years of history.

The slapstick humor of Kyōgen contrasts sharply with the meditative nature of Noh theater, and the best part of it is that we can confirm we share a sense of humor with people who lived centuries ago 😁. 

A classic Kyōgen play called “Bonsan” is about a thief who sneaks into an acquaintance’s house to steal a Bonsai because he wasn’t satisfied with the ones he owned himself. 

At night, the thief successfully breaks into the acquiantance’s place. While he struggles to choose which beautiful Bonsai to take, the owner of the house comes home with a sword in his hand and notices someone’s hiding. 

“Who’s there 😠!?” hollered the owner of the house, but just to see what the thief will do, he continues cunningly, “…Or perhaps it’s just a dog.” 

Then, having no better idea to get away, the thief goes, “…Ruff ruff! Ruff ruff!”

“Oh, it’s just a dog. …Or maybe 😏, it’s a monkey.”
“……Oo oo aa aa!! Oo oo aa aa!!!”

“(Laughing inside 😂) …Or maybe, it’s a fish 😏.”
“……(FISH!?!? HOW DO FISH CRY😖!?) 

“If it’s not a fish, it must be a thief. I will have to bring my gun and shoot the bejesus out of him 😤.”
“……FISH FISH! FISH FISH 😫😫😫!”
“Okay you pathetic maggot! Come over here 😂!!”

And they run off from the stage. The end 😂.

Viewed Whether a fruit is keto-approved depends on its carbohydrates and fiber count. Because fiber buffers the impact of carbs on your blood sugar, high-fiber fruits, like berries, can be a great way to add some natural sweetness to your keto diet without kicking you out of ketosis.

Berries are naturally high in fiber and keto-friendly. But you must be aware of their net carbs and include them in your daily net carb count.

Understanding the net carbs of fruits and berries is crucial for a successful keto diet. Total carbs and net carbs are two different things.

The total carbs of any food combine fiber and sugars. But because fiber has no impact on your blood sugar, you can subtract fiber from the total carb count to get a precise net carb amount. Limit your daily net carb intake to no more than 50 grams to stay in ketosis.

Avoiding most fruits won’t negatively affect your vitamin and mineral levels. Keto-approved vegetables and berries provide your body with all the essential nutrients needed for your health. Bell peppers and leafy greens like kale have more than double the amount of vitamin C compared to an orange.

Then we made this colossal mistake...
(A story about Quest Apparel's rise and fall.)

Quest Nutrition exploded out of the gate. 

The company was born on the back of a mindset, and we wanted our customers to know that too. 

So we launched a lifestyle apparel brand around the relentless pursuit of maximizing your human potential. The brand was aggressive and cool.

So why haven’t you ever heard of it? 

Because we shut it down.
It failed. Hard.

But why?

Quest Nutrition was a brand built on completely different things. 

It was about junk food that happened to be good for you. It was a health-conscious food brand largely for people who wanted to lose weight.

Quest Apparel didn’t resonate with our customers at all. 

What Quest meant to me as a founder, was not what it meant to the consumer... and only the consumer matters. 

It suddenly became clear to me that Quest launching a clothing company was like Quaker Oats launching a clothing company. You may love Quaker Oats, but do you want to wear an upscale $120 henley made by them?

No. That’s just not what you have in your head when you think of them.

If you stay true to your brand’s core, understand your audience, create straight lines (see my previous posts for a step by step process), and always build the audience before you create the product... you’ll be able to evolve your business. 

But if you don’t do that, you’re going to burn a lot of money. 
Take it from someone who’s burned millions, so you don’t have to.
